new_statements.rule_in_words: Agar (South Central) Dinka is described as a tone language (H, L, F on the single vowel of a largely monosyllabic word) with contrastive vowel length and voice quality; none of Andersen's accessible Agar descriptions (1992, 2017, 2020, 2023, 2025) mentions word stress at all. The only accent-placement remarks come from the two 19th-century Holy Cross mission grammars of the Ciec/Kyec variety: Beltrame 1869 p. 239 says the written accents mark vowel quality/length and that 'where the accent falls the rest of the voice (posa della voce) must also fall', specifying case by case which vowel carries it, his examples all being the last vowel (uen-e, gon-ter, ke-piat p. 241); Mitterrutzner 1866 sec. 15 p. 12 says polysyllabic words without tone marks have all syllables at the same pitch, and p. 20 that in ke- abstract nouns 'der Ton ruht immer auf der letzten Silbe'. No general word-stress rule is stated by any opened source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Beltrame 1869 p. 239 (Italian): 'Ove cade l'accento dovra pur cadere la posa della voce; che se talvolta dovetti accentare piu d'una vocale, nella stessa parola, per determinarne i suoni, dissi pero sempre fra parentesi, su quale vocale deve cadere la posa della voce: p. e. uen-e questo fanciullo; gon-ter da molto tempo (la voce posa sull'ultima vocale).' = 'Where the accent falls, the rest of the voice must also fall; when I had to accent more than one vowel in the same word to fix their sounds, I always said in parentheses on which vowel the rest of the voice must fall, e.g. uen-e this boy; gon-ter long ago (the voice rests on the last vowel).' Mitterrutzner 1866 p. 12 (German): 'Sind die Vokale eines mehrsilbigen Wortes mit keinem Tonzeichen versehen, so gilt die Regel, dass alle Silben die gleiche Tonhoehe haben' = 'If the vowels of a polysyllabic word bear no tone mark, the rule is that all syllables have the same pitch'; p. 20: 'Bei diesen abstrakten Substantiven ruht der Ton immer auf der letzten Silbe' = 'In these (ke-) abstract nouns the accent always rests on the last syllable.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Dinka roots are monosyllabic (Andersen 1992 sec. 2), polysyllables being prefixed/compound forms, which is why stress is not a live category in the modern descriptions. Beltrame and Mitterrutzner describe the Kyec/Ciec (Holy Cross mission) variety in 1860s missionary notation, with 'accento'/'Ton' covering vowel quality, length and pitch as well as prominence; Andersen describes Agar (Rumbek).
new_statements.identity_note: Andersen's papers describe the Agar dialect (Rumbek area), which Glottolog places under South Central Dinka sout2833. Mitterrutzner 1866 and Beltrame 1869 describe the Dinka of the Heiligkreuz/Holy Cross mission among the Kyec (Ciec) tribe at 6 deg 40' N on the west bank of the White Nile (Mitterrutzner pp. XI-XII), i.e. the Ciec variety of South Central Dinka (dialect-level glottocode not verified). Luanyjang/Rek (Remijsen & Manyang 2009, Remijsen & Ladd 2008, Nebel 1948) and Bor (Remijsen 2013, van Urk 2015) materials held under sout2832/sout2834 are other Dinka languages and were not used here.

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Andersen 1992-1994 statement: tone language (Agar has three tonemes), no stress statement. Adds that the TBU is the syllable and that the /a-/ noun prefix is toneless.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka (Agar included, with Agar data supplied by Torben Andersen, p. 15) is described as a predominantly monosyllabic tone language in which almost every syllable carries lexical tone and the tone-bearing unit is the syllable; the only toneless syllable type is the noun prefix /a-/. The word 'stress' never occurs in the body of the thesis. Its only appearances are in the bibliography (Gilley 2003 'The feature of stress in Nilotic'; Hualde et al. 2002), and Gilley 2003 is cited on p. 8 only as one of several publications that 'do not take work on tone into consideration, some of which are misleading'.
new_statements.exceptions: Toneless prefix /a-/ in a class of disyllabic nouns (fn. 2 p. 5; p. 28); polysyllabic words otherwise mostly loans (p. 28).
new_statements.identity_note: Blum 2023 is a cross-variety study of five dialects (Ngok, Bor South, Twic, Luanyjang, Agar); its Agar data come from Torben Andersen and it cites Andersen 1987/1992-1994 for Agar. Remijsen 2010 covers eight dialects and names Agar explicitly as a three-toneme dialect (after Andersen 1987); its word-structure and sandhi examples are mostly from Luanyjang, Bor, Nyarweng and Ruweng, with Agar treated on slides 29-48. Neither describes a variety other than Dinka, but neither is an Agar-only description.

new_statements.quote: [slide 10] The great majority of Dinka words consists of closed monosyllables, e.g.: bîɲ cup.SG, mjɛ̀ɛɛr giraffe.PL. Native polysyllabic words invariably begin with /a-/, and end in a closed syllable, e.g.: aɲáaar buffalo.SG, adò̤ok gourd.PL. Only the final syllable carries tone phonologically. [slide 29] Three dialects of Dinka have only 3 tonemes: - Western Twic - Ruweng - Agar (Andersen 1987) [slide 34] In Ruweng (3T) and Agar (3T), *H and *HL have neutralised: both are falling in final position and high elsewhere.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (world-r2) has an empty rule; the existing statement (Andersen 1992) reads tone language, three vowel lengths, no stress statement. Gilley agrees Dinka is tonal and monosyllabic-rooted and supplies no stress placement; what she adds is an analytic claim that the extra-short vs short (and short vs long) durational contrast is 'stress' rather than a third length degree. That differs in TYPE from Andersen's ternary-length analysis (she says so herself, p. 10) but not in any placement, so for word-stress position it is compatible: the locus of her 'stress' is always the monosyllabic root. Prior passes recorded that Blum 2023 (p. 8) lists Gilley 2003 'The feature of stress in Nilo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is described as tonal (two level tones plus HF, LF and Rise contours, p. 11) with mostly monosyllabic CVC roots. Gilley's 'stress' is not a positional word-stress rule: it is her label for a paradigmatic contrast on the monosyllabic root in which the 'stressed' word has a vowel about half the length of its 'unstressed' counterpart, explicitly a relabelling of Andersen's (1993) three degrees of vowel length as two lengths plus stress (p. 10: Andersen 'proposes three degrees of length, a concept totally rejected by the Dinka themselves.. The term stress has been used to distinguish the length variations between extra short and short and between short and long'). The contrast carries grammatical load (2ps vs 3ps readers, focus, singular vs plural nouns, exx. 1-7, 41-53); where a stress mark is written it precedes the root syllable, never the a- prefix (a'moc). Orthographically speakers mark the UNstressed word with a final apostrophe (p. 10). No statement about which syllable of a polysyllable is stressed, none on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None as a placement rule. Notes: ex. (43) roots with an underlying short vowel cannot lengthen, so singular is 'extra short' vs plural 'just short' or 'lowered' (Duerksen 1989); long-vowel verbs (exx. 6-7) sound 'like a short vowel that has no stress' (referred to Miller and Gilley 2001).
new_statements.identity_note: Gilley 2004's Dinka examples are from the Rek dialect (Southwestern Dinka, dik), collected with Lino Kiir; she states Rek 'is representative of all dialects: Rek, Bor, Agaar, and Padang' (p. 4), and the SIL archive entry lists South Central Dinka [dib] among the subject languages. The catalog item is Agar (South Central Dinka, sout2833); Andersen's works and Remijsen 2010 describe Agar directly.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the sources opened: Blum 2023 and Remijsen 2010 both treat Dinka (Agar included) as a predominantly monosyllabic tone language with the syllable as TBU and make no stress statement, matching the existing Andersen 1992-1994 statement. One latent conflict lies in the unopened Gilley line of work: Remijsen & Manyang 2009 (JIPA, fn. 5, read in the sibling directory) report that Gilley 2003 analyses the morphological quantity distinction in Dinka as a separate phonological contrast called 'stress' (short morphological grade = +stress), which Remijsen & Gilley 2008 found no acoustic evidence for in Luanyjang, and which Blum 2023 (p. 8) lists among publications that are 'misleading' because they ignore tone. Gilley 2004 (SIL EWP 2004-003) could not be opened, so whether it repeats the stress analysis for Dinka orthography is unverified. One analytic disagreement, not a placement conflict: Gilley 2004 (pp. 5, 10) calls the Dinka extra-short vs short (and short vs long) vowel contrast 'stress' ('Stressed words in Dinka shorten the vowel to about half its original length.. The term stress has been used to distinguish the length variations'), rejecting Andersen's (1987, 1993) three contrastive vowel lengths, which Andersen 1992/2017/2025, Remijsen 2010 and Blum 2023 all adopt for Agar (Blum 2023 p. 8 lists Gilley 2003 on Nilotic 'stress' among misleading publications). Gilley's 'stress' sits on the monosyllabic root and marks grammatical categories; no source stat…
